A proposed design for a back reflector in thin-film photovoltaics utilizes a three-dimensional photonic band gap back reflector to boost the absorption of light within a photovoltaic material. The effectiveness of these back reflectors relies on coupling with waveguide modes in the photovoltaic material. Theoretical calculations show that a 100 nm thick silicon layer can reach an absorption level of 90% at a specific wavelength when combined with a 3D photonic band gap back reflector, surpassing the absorption capability of a similar silicon layer with a conventional metal back reflector.

This study reveals a series of complex-valued, continuously differentiable functions that satisfy the iterative exponentiation property to any degree, while being transcendently dependent on their base value. Additionally, we prove the existence of numerous other solutions to the iterative exponentiation equation, characterized by a set of free parameters.

We've developed a novel method for constructing high-dimensional expanders, leveraging group theory and covering spaces. Our approach utilizes a collection of finite groups with subgroups, where the groups' properties enable the creation of exceptional expander structures. By generating these groups through random processes, we achieve a more efficient and versatile framework for high-dimensional expansion. This breakthrough has significant implications for theoretical computer science and quantum computing, opening up new avenues for research and potential applications.

The crystal structure of the magnetic material GdInO$_3$ has been determined, and its magnetic properties have been studied. The compound exhibits two distinct magnetic phase transitions at 162 K and 149 K, respectively. The first transition corresponds to the establishment of long-range antiferromagnetic order, whereas the second transition is associated with a spin reorientation. The magnetic structure of GdInO$_3$ has been identified as a type-II antiferromagnet, with the magnetic moments of the Gd$^{3+}$ ions aligned within the ab plane. The results of this study are in agreement with theoretical predictions and provide a foundation for further research into the magnetic properties of this class of materials.

A crucial task in network analysis is link prediction, which involves identifying potential connections between network nodes. This task becomes particularly challenging in large-scale networks with millions of nodes and billions of edges, where traditional methods struggle to provide accurate predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach called Sparse Structure Network Embedding (SSNE), which efficiently represents network nodes to facilitate link prediction. By focusing on the sparse nature of these networks, SSNE enables the consideration of local network structures and the preservation of network sparsity in the embedded space. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of network datasets, surpassing existing methods in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, SSNE demonstrates its scalability on very large-scale networks, such as those with tens of millions of nodes and billions of edges.

A low-cost, high-performance silicon micro-machined deep vapor cell is presented. Utilizing standard micro-machining techniques, the deep cell exhibits high figure of merit performance, comparable to that of traditional glass-mercury sealed cells. The performance evaluation includes measurements of line width, cell robustness, and temperature dependence. The results indicate a high figure of merit of 0.16, comparable to that of traditional glass-mercury sealed cells, and a long lifetime of over 1000 days. The error field sensitivity is also comparable to that of traditional glass-mercury sealed cells, with a long-term lifetime of over 1000 days.

We present a novel approach to modeling the impact of nonlinear interference in 
complex optical transmission systems, specifically for advanced dual-polarization 
4D formats. This model, referred to as the FourD-GNL model, is built upon a 
previously established framework known as the GN model. Experimental results 
demonstrate that the FourD-GNL model closely matches actual measurements, with 
a high degree of accuracy, outperforming predictions made by the traditional 
GN model.

A cutting-edge, deep learning-based method called FIRe-GAN is presented for fusing visible and infrared images of wildfires. This innovative approach leverages Generative Adversarial Networks to enhance the fusion process, surpassing traditional techniques. By leveraging GANs' ability to learn complex patterns in image data, FIRe-GAN achieves superior results in preserving the essential features of the input images, particularly in the context of wildfire monitoring. Extensive testing on various datasets demonstrates the efficacy of FIRe-GAN in improving image fusion quality, paving the way for more effective wildfire detection and analysis.

This research outlines the development of a dataset for identifying indicators of depression in social media posts, along with the outcomes of experiments utilizing this data to train machine learning models. Our dataset is unique in that it comprises social media posts verified as depicting signs of depression by human evaluators, rather than being labeled based on confirmed depression diagnoses. Our findings indicate that a combination of word embeddings and BERT, paired with a Long Short-Term Memory network, achieved the highest accuracy in detecting signs of depression on average, reaching 80.4% precision on the development set. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the performance of our model is consistent with that of a model trained on the Twitter Depression dataset, suggesting that our developed dataset is a valuable resource for further research into depression detection on social media.

This study presents a stochastic model of the COVID-19 pandemic, based on the dynamics of an SIR-type model, and investigates its properties in a coherent state space. The model's characteristics are then applied to real-world data from the United States, and it is found that certain parameters can be accurately estimated using a Markov chain, but others remain difficult to determine.

This research aims to explore the impact of isoscalar quadrupole strength connections on the behavior of the isoscalar giant monopole resonance (ISGMR) in magnesium-24 and silicon-28. Using the self-consistent Skyrme Hartree-Fock-RPA approach, we find that the interaction between the ISGMR and the isoscalar quadrupole giant resonance (ISGQR) results in a notable shift in the energy of the ISGMR to lower levels and a broadening of its distribution. Furthermore, we discover that the ISGMR's strength is significantly redistributed into the ISGQR, with the RPA wave functions showing a substantial contribution from quadrupole configurations. This effect is more pronounced in magnesium-24 than in silicon-28, with the ISGMR's energy in magnesium-24 being notably reduced by the ISGQR interaction. Our findings align with experimental data, with the calculated ISGMR energies for magnesium-24 and silicon-28 closely matching their respective measured values.

This study examines the impact of feedback control on stick-slip instabilities in mechanical systems subject to Coulomb friction. The research establishes that for systems with smooth, bounded feedback control, the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the resulting differential inclusions are guaranteed, and that solutions to these systems converge over time. The findings are illustrated through two examples: a simple model of a friction-driven pendulum and a more complex, nonlinear suspension system.

A novel reinforcement learning approach, Deep Bellman Hedging, has been developed to tackle the challenge of learning optimal policies in complex environments efficiently. This method addresses the limitations of traditional reinforcement learning algorithms, which often struggle to converge and require extensive trial-and-error interactions. By leveraging a Bellman-style hedging technique, Deep Bellman Hedging achieves faster learning rates and more stable convergence. This approach has been successfully applied to both tabular and deep learning-based settings, yielding significant improvements in convergence speed and sample efficiency.

In the field of sequential recommender systems, accurately modeling user intent is crucial. Current approaches, however, often rely on explicit user feedback like item interactions, which can be sparse and noisy. This research proposes a novel method for implicit intent modeling using a two-stage process. Initially, it extracts latent user signals from online behavior, such as browsing history, and then incorporates these signals into a sequential recommender via attention mechanisms. This approach is tested on a large-scale dataset and demonstrates significant improvements in both online and offline evaluations.

The reducible double confluent Heun equation is linked to a specific unfolding of the Dirichlet-Laplace operator's differential equation, and also to a specific unfolding of Lame's equation, which has a general potential that has symmetric elliptic function characteristics.

Low-rank matrix recovery has been the subject of extensive research in various fields, including statistics and machine learning. Focusing on a specific scenario, we investigate estimating matrices with low ranks where data is gathered from independent Gaussian distributions, but noise levels vary across different matrix entries. This heterogeneity is described by the concept of groupwise heteroskedasticity. Our analysis centers on the task of identifying the sign of the largest singular value of a given matrix. We establish that when the signal strength is weak, accurate estimation is impossible, whereas for stronger signals, we establish a lower bound on the mean-squared error of our estimators. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a specific Bayesian estimator is nearly optimal in this context.

In the study of topological insulators, we've developed a new intrinsic model that doesn't rely on any particular crystal structure. This model is based on the concept of a two-band Hamiltonian and can be applied to any system with two energy levels. We've also derived conditions that need to be met for a topological phase to occur, and we've shown how our model is related to the Chern number and the Zak phase. Additionally, we've used numerical simulations to study the properties of topological insulators in two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems.

The lepton flavor universality ratio in semi-inclusive $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions is investigated, where the sum of lepton pairs includes both electrons and muons. The analysis is carried out within the Standard Model using the soft-collinear effective theory. The results are compared to recent experimental data from the LHCb collaboration, which shows agreement with the theoretical model's predictions. The study also reveals that the universality ratio is sensitive to the dimension-eight operators, which become dominant at small hadronic invariant mass values.

This paper addresses the issue of designing distributed control systems for interconnected systems, where each agent in the network operates independently without access to other agents' information. The challenge lies in creating a distributed control system that achieves global stability, even in the presence of uncertain system parameters. To overcome this, we introduce a new design framework that leverages only local information and independent local computations. The proposed framework enables the creation of a distributed control system that is stable and robust, regardless of the network's structure or the channel dimensions. The control gains can be efficiently computed using standard eigenvalue-based methods, and the approach can be applied to various interconnected systems, such as those found in power grids and chemical processes. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through numerical examples, which show its ability to achieve stable operation and efficient energy usage.

A novel dual-layer COVID19 classification system has been developed to enhance the accuracy of diagnostic outcomes. The proposed framework integrates the power of BERT technology with a conventional machine learning model to provide a comprehensive diagnostic tool. By leveraging BERT's ability to extract and process language features, the first layer of the system employs a text-based interface to collect and analyze patient information. These extracted features are then utilized to train a BERT model, which generates essential input for the second layer of the system. The second layer consists of a Random Forest classifier, which uses the BERT-generated features to make diagnostic decisions. The proposed framework's efficacy has been demonstrated through comparative analysis with other machine learning models, showcasing its superior performance.

This comprehensive guide is an all-inclusive resource for network scientists, featuring a wide array of essential tools and software for creating, examining, and analyzing networks. It provides in-depth descriptions of cutting-edge platforms and software, including those for network representation, such as Graphviz, Gephi, and NetworkX, as well as network analysis tools like igraph, and Jupyter notebooks. Furthermore, the guide covers cutting-edge software for cutting-edge network analysis tasks, such as cutting-edge network visualization tools, cutting-edge network analysis software, and cutting-edge platforms for cutting-edge network research. It also includes cutting-edge software for cutting-edge network research tasks, such as cutting-edge network analysis tools, cutting-edge network research software, and cutting-edge platforms for cutting-edge network research.

Theoretical frameworks in eco-evolutionary dynamics often focus on specific processes, such as evolutionary change or ecological interactions, but rarely consider their interconnected nature. This study develops a unified framework to analyze the long-term impact of coupled eco-evolutionary dynamics, considering the timescales and factors influencing these processes. An analytical model demonstrates that the timescale ratio between ecological and evolutionary dynamics determines whether populations reach equilibrium, while also revealing the importance of modulators like growth rates and selection rates. This framework offers a comprehensive approach to understanding eco-evolutionary dynamics across various timescales and biological systems.

Recent self-supervised learning methods for speech have shown potential in speech recognition tasks, but their resistance to malicious attacks remains poorly understood. To investigate this vulnerability, a study was conducted using three speech self-supervised models on the IS2 attack platform. The results indicate that these models are susceptible to specific types of attacks, with speech features being easily compromised, resulting in significant performance degradation. Furthermore, a characterisation of the relationship between self-supervised pretraining objectives and susceptibility to attacks was achieved. The findings suggest that the statistical mode of speech signals may offer better resistance to attacks, which could inform the design of more robust speech features.

The cryptocurrency market has seen significant growth in recent years, with trading volumes reaching unprecedented levels.  Despite the remarkable expansion, the field remains poorly understood.  This paper investigates the reasons behind the adoption of decentralized exchanges, a key player in the cryptocurrency ecosystem.  By applying the technology acceptance model, our analysis reveals that users primarily adopt these exchanges for the perceived benefits they offer.  Furthermore, we find that users' trust in these exchanges is a crucial factor in their adoption.  Our results have significant implications for the cryptocurrency industry, with the potential to inform the development of more user-friendly and trustworthy decentralized exchanges.

A new method is developed to quantify the impact of unverified assumptions on statistical inferences in the presence of missing data. This approach utilizes a set of sensitivity parameters to model the missing data's hidden characteristics and generates an E-curve that represents various levels of confidence interval width or test statistic significance. By parameterizing the likelihood of a sensitivity parameter, an sensitivity analysis measure is established that indicates the degree of assumption validity needed to achieve a desired statistical result. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation studies and real-world applications, including a study on the effect of maternal age on children's risk of leukemia and a study on the effect of aspirin use on the risk of heart attacks.

This study concludes a comprehensive listing of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries for the Laurent extension of the quantum plane, denoted as $\mathcal{A}_q$, which was initiated in [arXiv:2001.01049]. We identify and categorize two distinct types of symmetries: those that can be expressed using the standard generators of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ and those that exhibit a more complex structure involving additional generators.

The convergence of Blockchain and Internet of Vehicles technologies has significant implications for various vehicle applications, such as autonomous driving and smart city infrastructure. A proposed framework, combining Federated Learning and Distributed Ledger Technology, has the potential to revolutionize these applications by addressing challenges like data privacy and resource allocation. A comprehensive review of this framework, however, reveals gaps in existing research, particularly in areas like resource management and consensus mechanisms. This study aims to fill these gaps by providing an in-depth analysis of the framework's current state and identifying future research directions to advance its development and implementation.

The differential cross-sections for beauty and charm creation in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV are examined using data from the CMS detector at the LHC. The analysis is based on a sample of 20.3 inverse nanobarns of integrated data. Two distinct methods of identifying beauty and charm particles are employed: one for prompt charm creation and one for non-prompt charm and beauty creation through the decay of heavy particles into D mesons. The results are presented in terms of transverse momentum and rapidity for both D mesons and D mesons resulting from beauty and charm production. The results are compared with theoretical predictions and measurements from previous experiments.

Our team has developed a large-scale platform for creating and testing superconducting qubits at quantum computing facilities. The platform is housed at the Fermilab Quantum Information Science Center and features an advanced dilution refrigerator capable of holding 1,000 qubits, along with 12 custom-designed input/output racks. Each rack accommodates 80 wires, allowing for flexible and organized connections to individual qubits. The platform also includes a custom-designed software suite to manage and control qubit operations, as well as the necessary hardware to execute those operations. The platform's capabilities were demonstrated through the testing of multiple qubit circuits, including both basic and more complex architectures.

Cryptographic tools are now integral to modern software, safeguarding sensitive data and maintaining user trust. However, misusing these tools poses a significant risk, as it can lead to data breaches and loss of user confidence. This study focuses on identifying and analyzing common misconfigurations of cryptographic libraries in Java and Python, by examining a large collection of vulnerable Java code and developing a similar dataset for Python. Our research highlights the prevalence of these misconfigurations, such as using outdated or weak encryption methods, and provides guidance on preventing and mitigating them.

Automatically labelling large-scale datasets is a complex task, and we propose a decentralized approach that doesn't rely on centralized human annotation. By utilizing decentralized human input, our method can be easily adapted to various domains and domains, and we demonstrate its effectiveness on two datasets of different sizes. The key advantage of our approach lies in its ability to handle large datasets without requiring extensive storage space, and we also explore the impact of our approach on dataset quality and size.

In seismic data processing, sparse inversion of reflectivity is a widely used technique that effectively handles noisy data and mitigates ringing effects. However, the conventional l1-norm regularization often yields non-ideal results, particularly in cases where the sparsity of the reflectivity is non-uniform. This paper proposes a new method for reflectivity inversion that utilizes a non-convex and non-uniform sparse model, proximal to the l2-norm, to enhance the inversion process. The proposed method, NuSPAN, is a network architecture that utilizes proximal average functions to approximate the target non-convex function, and is shown to converge to a stationary point under mild conditions. The proposed NuSPAN network outperforms existing methods in terms of inversion accuracy and yield in sparse reflectivity inversion.

This study examines the behavior of iterated semigroups of composition operators on spaces analogous to BMOA, including those characterized by weighted L^2 integrals with semi-definite kernels of the form (1 - |z|)^{2s}(1-|\langle z,\zeta\rangle|^2)^{s_1}, where s, s_1 ≥ 0. It also investigates the semigroup of operators defined by (I-z\bar{\zeta})^{-1}f(z) and (I+z\bar{\zeta})^{-1}f(z) for s_1 = 0, consisting of operators related to Poisson integrals and the Cauchy kernel. The findings establish that the semigroup of composition operators associated with (I-z\bar{\zeta})^{-1}f(z) and (I+z\bar{\zeta})^{-1}f(z) converges weakly to the identity operator in the unit ball for s_1 = 0, while that associated with (I-z\bar{\zeta})^{-1}f(z) converges to 0 for s_1 = 0. The work further identifies the maximal range of s_1 for which the semigroup of composition operators associated with (I-z\bar{\zeta})^{-1}f(z) converges to 0 for s_1 = 0.

We have developed a method to calculate the scaling dimensions and universal components of relevant scaling operators within minimal models using numerical wavefunction analysis. Our approach reveals the presence of universal finite-size effects that can be accurately predicted through a scaling hypothesis, thereby eliminating the necessity for extrapolations in small system sizes. By applying this methodology, we have derived universal scaling dimensions and identified the complete set of relevant operators, including their coefficients, for the critical Haagerup model.

We introduce an innovative approach to historical language analysis that addresses the lack of reliable annotated data in historical corpora. By acknowledging the annotation errors inherent in such data, our method employs set-valued prediction to provide a range of plausible tags for each word. This technique is applied to part-of-speech tagging and has been successfully tested on Old High German texts from two distinct periods, utilizing two distinct prediction models. The results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms traditional taggers in handling historical languages, with average F1 scores of 60-70% for settings that account for errors. Furthermore, our method allows for the extraction of multiple, annotated versions of texts, which can then be used to create robust tags and provide valuable insights into historical language usage.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for handling non-smooth non-concave integrals, providing a bridge between discrete and continuous models. Key concepts such as subgradients, momentum, and their relationships with dual spaces are rigorously defined. These theories are applied to develop a variational framework that accommodates non-smooth, non-convex integrands and their associated dual problems. Ultimately, this framework enables the derivation of a Hamiltonian system for a broad class of discrete and continuous models.

This study presents a pioneering approach to automatically translating requirements specified in urban development plans into a formal specification using the City Requirements Ontology (CRO). CRO is an innovative framework that defines essential elements and attributes of urban developments. CRO enables the representation of relationships between these elements, which is crucial for accurately capturing the complexities of urban environments. Our methodology leverages a combination of natural language processing and knowledge representation techniques to facilitate this translation process. Our results demonstrate that this approach can significantly reduce the time and effort required for converting city requirements into a formal specification, thereby facilitating more efficient urban development planning.

A significant challenge in developing large-scale quantum computers is the presence of errors in quantum gates. To overcome this issue, error mitigation techniques have been developed to improve the accuracy of quantum computations. In this research, we introduce a new error mitigation approach called the hidden inverses protocol, which utilizes a quantum circuit's inherent inverse structure to counteract errors. By applying this protocol to a superconducting quantum processor, we successfully demonstrated its effectiveness in mitigating errors in single-qubit gates and quantum gates involving two qubits. Furthermore, we observed that the hidden inverses protocol outperforms other gate-based error mitigation methods when used in complex quantum algorithms.

In a general category $\mathcal E$ that supports finite limits, we investigate the behavior of a function $f: A \to B$ when it has the ability to handle weakly regular functions. Specifically, we demonstrate that in such a category, $f$ can be considered weakly regular if and only if it preserves certain structures, namely, it must be true that for any given strong preorder or equivalence relation on $A$, $f$ can be extended to a cocartesian morphism.

The application of multivariate spatial models to real-world data is explored, specifically data collected from the North Sea. This analysis utilizes a multivariate non-stationary extreme value model to model joint sea surface height and wave height data. This model is applied to two distinct areas of the North Sea: the Dogger Bank and the Dogger Bank South. By modeling the data, researchers can estimate the probability of exceeding specific thresholds and calculate return periods for extreme events. This approach enables a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between sea surface height and wave height, as well as the dependence between these variables at different locations.

Recent advancements in vision-language models have led to breakthroughs in various computer vision tasks, but these models are often vulnerable to spurious correlations in training data, resulting in flawed predictions. To address this issue, we introduce VT-CLIP, a new approach that refines the original CLIP model by incorporating an attention mechanism to incorporate text-based visual details. By doing so, VT-CLIP can improve the robustness of the CLIP model against distributional shifts and enhance its performance on various tasks, including zero-shot classification and image retrieval.

We develop efficient strategies to mitigate noise in matrix-based systems, leveraging the approximation of perturbed matrices by their underlying, uncorrupted counterparts. Our approach, grounded in the Singular Perturbation Theorem, provides an alternative to traditional denoising techniques like Principal Component Analysis and the Empirical Bayesian framework. The theoretical foundation of this method is established through the characterization of a class of operators that facilitate noise suppression. The empirical efficacy of our operator-shifting methodology is demonstrated through its application to a variety of systems, including numerical examples and real-world datasets.

We calculate the slices and the slice spectral sequence of spectra of Eilenberg-Mac Lane type in dimensions $2$ and $3$ with coefficients in the quaternions. This is achieved by adapting techniques from previous research on the slices of the 2-dimensional Moore spectrum, and then applying them to the quaternionic context.

Given a Noetherian local ring, we establish a link between its tight Hilbert polynomial and its formal fiber local rings' $F$-rationality. This connection allows us to demonstrate that if the tight Hilbert polynomial of a $d$-dimensional $F$-rational local ring exhibits a degree of $2d-2$ or less, then every formal fiber local ring is also $F$-rational. This finding is particularly significant in two- and three-dimensional cases. Additionally, we provide specific instances demonstrating that our result is the strongest possible outcome in the two-dimensional scenario.

The integration of deep learning in medical imaging has seen significant advancements in recent years, with numerous research papers reporting outstanding diagnostic accuracy in various medical fields. However, the results of these studies often face challenges due to inconsistencies in data analysis pipelines, a lack of reproducibility, and difficulties in comparing and validating model performance. To address these issues, there is a pressing need for a unified approach to model evaluation and exchange. In response, the DICOM standard has been expanded with the introduction of the "structured transfer syntax" for encapsulating application-specific data, such as deep learning model outputs in medical imaging, within DICOM files. This has led to the development of highdicom, a Python library designed to facilitate the creation of compliant code for deep learning applications in medical imaging. This article outlines the highdicom functionality and presents its initial validation outcomes, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability and scalability of deep learning models in medical imaging.

We consider the variation of Noether currents, corresponding to diffeomorphisms, for the Einstein-Hilbert action's surface term. This involves imposing specific boundary conditions on the currents, which yield a central charge, corresponding to a Virasoro algebra. The central charge is found to be directly proportional to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy, with both being functions of the AdS radius and the gravitational constant.

In the field of genomics, unsupervised learning has gained significant attention, 
particularly in the analysis of DNA sequences. This research focuses on developing 
a novel, unsupervised method for learning DNA representations that can be applied 
to both DNA sequence classification and variant calling. The new representation 
model, known as DNN-Embed, is an extension of Word2Vec that enables the creation of 
informative DNA representations without relying on labeled data. By comparing its 
performance to other leading models, such as k-mer, CNN, and Transformer, our 
experiments demonstrate that DNN-Embed outperforms them in both DNA classification 
and variant calling tasks.

The phase transition between metal and insulator states in V$_2$O$_3$ is influenced by the termination of its surface layers. By growing V$_2$O$_3$ films on different substrates, we observed that films grown on Bi$_2$O$_3$ remained in an insulating state, whereas those grown on Bi$_2$WO$_9$ exhibited a metal-like temperature dependence in their electrical conductivity. Our analysis revealed that variations in the film's surface structure, specifically the arrangement of vanadium atoms, are responsible for these differences. Furthermore, we found that the insulating state in V$_2$O$_3$ is linked to the presence of specific types of bonds within the material's crystal structure.

A new, systematic approach is developed to convert Lie-Poisson systems into their equivalent Clebsch form, which enables the use of additional variables to express Hamilton's equations. By employing this method, further variable transformations can be applied to simplify Lie-Poisson systems into simpler Hamilton-PDEs on lower-dimensional manifolds. This framework is particularly useful in fluid dynamics applications and is demonstrated through its application to the Euler equations on the Lie algebra of area-preserving vector fields and the Sophistocles model on so(3).

A fundamental property of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations lies in their ability to reduce to ODEs when the initial velocity field is zero, which is attributed to the existence of certain 'conserved quantities'. These quantities can be leveraged to derive key properties of the solutions, such as the uniform boundedness of the pressure and velocity gradient in specific function spaces. Notably, by eliminating the pressure through the vorticity, we can transform the equations into a system that preserves this property. This method can be extended to the study of the heat flux, which can be incorporated into the equations via the Stokes or Cattaneo model, resulting in the introduction of a new conserved quantity.

The assessment of machine learning models on complex financial datasets is a crucial task, especially in banking where they are widely used for tasks such as fraud prevention and credit risk assessment. This study compares the performance of linear and non-linear models on Normalized Power Loan Profile (NPLP) data, a dataset that is unique in its representation of loan information. Our analysis reveals that non-linear models, particularly Gradient Boosting and Random Forest, outperform linear models on NPLP data. Furthermore, we employed the SHAP method to extract and analyze the importance of features, revealing that model type significantly impacts the extraction of important features. Our findings emphasize the need for careful consideration of data characteristics and model type when evaluating machine learning models and selecting relevant features.

We've discovered a connection between the chromatic symmetric functions of certain Dyck paths and the theory of q-rooks. Our findings indicate that for specific Dyck paths, their chromatic symmetric functions can be broken down into the sum of q-rook polynomial sequences. This relationship allows us to identify a broader class of Dyck paths with this characteristic, which can be defined using the concept of "peaks" within the paths.

Deep learning models, specifically deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been widely used for various image recognition tasks. However, their performance is often hindered by the computational and data demands required to achieve high accuracy. To address this issue, researchers have developed more efficient CNN architectures that can learn from limited data and operate effectively on edge devices. A key challenge in this area is the need for novel designs that can effectively process images while maintaining high performance. To overcome this challenge, the authors propose the orientation convolutional network (ONet), a new CNN architecture that uses oriented kernels to capture the directional features of images. By leveraging the directional information in images, ONets can learn more efficient representations and outperform existing CNNs in various image classification tasks.

Using a novel relative trace formula, we investigate linear periods on $GL_{2n}$ that are modulated by a character with a twist. The key innovation in this process is the development of a relative fundamental lemma for quasi-invariant distributions, which serves as the essential groundwork for the application of the formula.

We have calculated the mass of the top quark in the context of quantum chromodynamics to a very high degree of accuracy, specifically including up to ten powers of the strong force coupling constant when considering the number of light quark flavors. This calculation is valid to a very high degree of accuracy, with an error margin of less than 0.1 MeV. This is achieved by using a mathematical framework that takes into account the strong force interactions between the quarks. This calculation is particularly important as it provides a more precise estimate of the mass of the top quark, which is a key parameter in the standard model of particle physics. This calculation is based on the work of several researchers, including the present authors, and provides a significant improvement over previous calculations. Consider an almost d-regular graph G, where each vertex has a degree that does not exceed d plus one. For any edge e, we can find a valid color assignment, where all edges connected to any vertex except the edge e, have distinct colors. This result holds true when the available palette of colors is sufficiently large, specifically when it contains at least 2d+1 colors. Moreover, we can also prove a similar result for vertex coloring in such graphs, where we can find a valid color assignment, where all edges connected to any vertex except the vertex itself, have distinct colors. This result holds true when the available palette of colors is sufficiently large, specifically when it contains at least 2d plus a small constant.

We establish a contractive inequality in weighted Bergman spaces for values of parameters between 0 and 1, which extends the findings of Beckner and relates to those of Coifman and Magg, in the latter's work on $L^p$ projections in spaces with dimension greater than or equal to 3.

This research presents a novel COVID-19 detection system based on low-dose computed tomography (CT) scans. To achieve accurate diagnosis, we developed a two-stage Time-distributed Capsule Network (TCN). The first stage utilizes TCN to identify pulmonary embolism, while the second stage focuses on identifying ground-glass opacities. By employing TCN in both stages, we are able to effectively model the temporal relationships within the pulmonary structures. Furthermore, our model's capsule network component allows for robust feature extraction and representation. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we conducted comprehensive experiments on the public COVID-19 dataset. The results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art models, achieving exceptional performance with an accuracy of 98.7%, precision of 98.6%, recall of 98.7%, and an AUC score of 98.7%.

As nations and corporations increasingly turn to space for services like satellite communications, navigation, and remote sensing, there's a growing need for sustainable space operations. This paper focuses on a critical aspect of space operations: managing the presence of space assets in a shared environment. We develop a mathematical model to quantify the presence of space objects in a specific region of orbit, and through simulations, we demonstrate the model's utility in analyzing the effects of varying orbital parameters. This tool can support decision-making in the management of Earth's Low-Earth Orbit, which is experiencing increased congestion due to a growing number of spacefaring entities.

CAD models are broken down into smaller, more detailed meshes to facilitate the creation of quad-based topological meshes. This is achieved by first dividing the models into coarse quad meshes, which are then refined into finer meshes. However, the current methods for creating these meshes often struggle with complex models, leading to inaccurate results. To address this issue, we propose a new approach that uses a novel energy function to optimize the placement of mesh vertices. This energy function takes into account the specific features of the model, such as its geometric and topological properties. By using a combination of integer programming techniques, we can efficiently create high-quality meshes for complex models. Our approach has been shown to outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The relationships between variables in time-series data change over different time periods. Researchers often use observations from the past to forecast these relationships in the future. A common approach involves predicting future correlations using the current estimated parameters. However, the accuracy of these predictions depends on the variability of the available data. This paper provides a mathematical solution to determine the expected value and variance of the sample correlation coefficient, which is a key element in time-series analysis. This mathematical solution is based on a detailed examination of the sample correlation coefficient, and it is derived using a step-by-step approach. The results of this paper are significant as they offer a deeper understanding of the time-varying nature of correlations in financial data, and they can be applied to a wide range of statistical and financial applications.

We detail the implementation of the causal S-matrix approach for solving three-dimensional and higher-dimensional Einstein's theory of gravity with cosmological constant, as well as its extensions to quadratic and higher-order gravity. Additionally, we outline the application of this method to Skyrme gravity and Einstein's theory coupled with a massive scalar field.

We establish the existence of finite dimensional interior localized feedback controls that stabilize the solutions of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in a domain $\Omega$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Specifically, our research demonstrates uniform stabilization in critical Sobolev and Besov spaces, denoted as $H^{1/2}(\Omega)$ and $B^{1/2}_{2,c}$, respectively. This result is a significant improvement over previous studies, which focused on the entire space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and employed feedback controls that were not localized.

Language learning dictionaries are essential tools for both native speakers and language learners.
Traditionally, dictionaries cater to established vocabulary, but LitMind Dictionary stands out by focusing on the most commonly used words in the language.
This dictionary is available online for free and can be integrated into other platforms.
It is continuously being updated with new entries, making it a valuable resource for language learners.
The project's code is open-source, allowing for community contributions and collaborations.

Recent developments in recommender systems have led to growing concerns about their transparency and fairness. To address these issues, researchers have created post-hoc explanation methods that can provide insights into how models make predictions. One such method, LIME, has been adapted for use in recommender systems, but it has limitations in providing accurate and trustworthy explanations. To overcome these limitations, we propose two novel post-hoc explanation metrics, Adherence and Constancy, to evaluate the reliability and consistency of LIME-RS explanations. Our experiments demonstrate that these metrics effectively capture the quality of explanations and can guide improvements to LIME-RS through the selection of optimal parameters.

The surface and interface Fermi level pinning in near-surface quantum wells pose significant challenges in developing high-performance semiconductor devices. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach to control Fermi level pinning in near-surface InAs quantum wells by adjusting their depth. Our experiments revealed that the depth of the quantum well has a significant impact on the position of the surface Fermi level, with deeper wells resulting in a shift towards the bandgap. Furthermore, we observed that increasing the well depth also reduces the density of interface dislocations, which in turn improves the quality of the material. Our findings demonstrate that the depth of the quantum well is a critical parameter in controlling Fermi level pinning and the quality of the material, with potential applications in the development of advanced semiconductor devices.

This paper investigates the robustness of learning using local exploration strategies. Local exploration involves examining and evaluating data points in close proximity to existing data points. This paper presents a new theoretical framework for analyzing the robustness of local exploration and demonstrates its effectiveness under realistic noise conditions. The framework's key insight is that local exploration is beneficial when a function's behavior can be accurately predicted by its behavior in close proximity. This leads to the conclusion that local exploration is effective in scenarios where the underlying data distribution is continuous, as well as in a variety of machine learning applications. The framework's implications are twofold: it provides a more accurate assessment of the robustness of local exploration and highlights the conditions under which it is effective.

Optimal transport problems are solved efficiently using the Sinkhorn algorithm, which relies on matrix multiplication. Fast algorithms for computing the product of structured matrices, particularly those with a specific pattern, enable accelerated convergence. Building on this concept, a new approach utilizes a specialized transform for a specific type of matrix to achieve faster computations. This approach, leveraging a linear time complexity, enables significant speed improvements in solving optimal transport problems.

Young stars like AU Microscopii are known to experience intense flares and emit strong far-ultraviolet radiation, which can significantly impact the evolution of nearby planets. To better understand this effect, astronomers observed AU Mic in quiescence and during two flares using the Hubble Space Telescope. The results showed that AU Mic's radiation output in the far-ultraviolet range increased dramatically during flares, reaching levels comparable to the Sun's in the visible spectrum. These findings have significant implications for understanding the evolution of nearby planets, including AU Mic's two known super-Earths, and suggest that intense flares could have a major impact on their atmospheres and atmospheres of similar planets in the future.

The impact of radiation emission on the motion of a point particle through a dissipative, non-conductive material is examined.  By analyzing the energy loss of the electromagnetic field in the far zone, it's discovered that the particle experiences a frictional force, which is proportional to the density of the surrounding medium and a factor of $c^5$, resulting in a drag-like effect.  The magnitude of this force is comparable to that of the Larmor force, but with opposite sign, implying that the surrounding medium can counteract the acceleration of the particle.  The presence of inertia in the electromagnetic field causes the frictional force to be independent of the acceleration, resulting in a terminal velocity for the particle, which is determined by the density of the surrounding medium and a factor of $c$.  The effects of the surrounding medium on the particle's motion are significant, and can lead to complex dynamics that are not present in the absence of the surrounding medium.

The effectiveness of the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) algorithm is heavily influenced by the proportion of rare classes in the dataset. Relying solely on the minority class ratio to determine the optimal k value is a common approach, but it is not always accurate. In this research, a statistical approach is developed to analyze the data distribution and assess the impact of the rare classes, allowing for a more informed selection of k. By utilizing this approach, a novel algorithm is created that outperforms the traditional kNN method, especially in datasets with significant minority classes.

We have identified 14 ultra-bright quasars from the early universe, discovered through the analysis of 10-band photometric data from the SkyMapper survey. These luminous quasars, characterized by their high brightness and redshifts exceeding 3.5, were selected based on their distinct color patterns. By combining our findings with previously known quasars, we have developed a new estimate of the quasar luminosity function, which reveals that the most luminous quasars are more abundant than previously thought. Our results indicate that there are likely more than 1000 extremely luminous quasars in the early universe, which could be found within the field of view of the James Webb Space Telescope.

We have developed a new experimental technique to study the charge-tunneling process between a quantum dot and a superconducting island. This technique allows us to monitor the superconducting island's charge state in real-time by using a sensing gate. By utilizing this approach, we can directly observe the quantum fluctuations of the dot-island system, which are not accessible through conventional transport measurements. Furthermore, we can demonstrate that these fluctuations are influenced by the dot's Cooper-pair tunneling, as well as by the dot's single-electron tunneling, and that these processes exhibit distinct characteristics.

We examine the contraction behavior of specific metrics for entropic discontinuities in linear and nonlinear hyperbolic systems. We establish that, for linear systems, a matrix of covariant Hessian is required to ensure contraction properties. We prove that, for nonlinear systems, a positive definite, symmetric, and monotone increasing Hessian matrix is necessary and sufficient to ensure contraction behavior. We also demonstrate the significance of these conditions through the example of the isentropic gas dynamics nonlinear system.

The diffusion model has revolutionized the field of image and video creation, offering a versatile framework for generating high-quality visual content. However, current video generation models struggle with maintaining consistency across frames, often resulting in unrealistic visual effects. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called DiffDreamer, which focuses on consistent view generation from a single image. By leveraging the inherent structure of 3D space, our model can produce realistic video sequences that accurately represent different camera angles. To further enhance the quality of our generated videos, we introduce a new training strategy called the latent feature replay method, which enables the model to learn and retain key visual features across frames. Through comprehensive experiments, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of DiffDreamer in producing high-quality, consistent video generation.

This paper introduces a novel, data-driven approach to predictive control for complex networks of processes. We utilize an agent-based model to simulate the interactions between network nodes, where each node represents a process influenced by its neighboring nodes. We use a data-driven method to forecast the behavior of individual nodes based on historical data, and then apply this prediction to optimize the control of the entire network, minimizing the impact of external disturbances. Our approach is tested on a model of disease spread, and the results show that it successfully mitigates the impact of disturbances on network dynamics.

The dynamics of a liquid film on a fiber are investigated, with a focus on how the liquid's surface tension instability is affected by the liquid's velocity at the film's surface. The analysis shows that when the liquid's surface is allowed to slip, the instability of the liquid's surface leads to the formation of larger droplets, with a higher slip velocity resulting in more pronounced droplet formation. The results are further validated through numerical simulations, with good agreement between the theoretical predictions and the simulations.

We demonstrate that the Hunter-Saxton equation exhibits Lipschitz stability in a suitable metric space. Moreover, this stability can be applied to various types of solutions, including those with finite variance. This finding has significant implications for the design of numerical schemes for the Hunter-Saxton equation.

Evaluating scoliosis curves using ultrasound is a reliable process that can be done consistently. Our research aimed to determine the reliability of robotic scanning compared to manual methods. We compared the reliability of scoliosis measurements from both robotic and human operators. We used ultrasound images from 20 patients with scoliosis and compared the angles measured by the ultrasound imaging system. We found that both robotic and human operators could produce consistent results. We concluded that the robotic scanning method is as reliable as human operators.

The text describes a median-based method for creating synthetic speech durations using a non-parametric approach, where the median is preferred over the mean due to its resistance to outliers in the training data. A new synthetic distribution is generated by combining the cumulative distribution functions of the original features, which are then used to sample the original durations. This process is applied to the TIMIT corpus and the results show that the synthetic durations have a median within the acceptable range for the majority of the phonemes, although some discrepancies remain.

The rise of social media has led to a surge in user participation, but this also brings with it the risk of negative behaviors such as spreading hate speech online. This study focuses on developing a predictive model for identifying hate speech on Facebook posts. A custom feature extraction method combining Word2Vec and Deep Neural Networks is employed to generate robust vector representations of words. These vectors are then used to build a machine learning classifier for identifying hate speech. By comparing the performance of the proposed model with existing techniques, this research aims to demonstrate the effectiveness of the developed approach in identifying hate speech on Facebook posts.

Deep neural networks, specifically Multi-input Multi-output (MIMO) networks, have been shown to excel in various tasks, particularly in image classification. These networks, characterized by their ability to share features across different input channels, have been found to be a key factor in their success. However, existing studies have primarily focused on quantifying the benefits of feature sharing, rather than exploring ways to optimize it. In this research, we delve into the effectiveness of feature sharing in MIMO architectures, specifically in the context of image classification. Our investigation reveals that not all layers within a MIMO network require feature sharing, and we propose a novel, adaptive method for determining the necessity of feature sharing in each layer. This method, which relies on the uncertainty of predictions, outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet.

The analysis of historical documents through image-based processing has been a significant area of research, driven by the need to unlock the content within these documents. This document focuses on providing an overview of existing historical document datasets, which are essential for advancing the field. By compiling a comprehensive list of available datasets, this document aims to serve as a reference guide for researchers working on historical document analysis.

This research paper presents an innovative flatness-based control approach for industrial robots, specifically focusing on a joint of the ABB IRB-1400 model. The proposed control law relies solely on data from the position controller and additional sensors, eliminating the need for external force sensors. The technique capitalizes on the robot's internal position controller feedback to determine the external force acting on the joint, effectively expanding the state space. The proposed control law's effectiveness is substantiated through theoretical analysis and demonstrated through experimental results on the specified industrial robot.

The study of longitudinal medical records has gained significant attention in recent years, with a focus on understanding how various health conditions evolve over time. This study proposes a new analytical framework, known as Multiple State Analysis, to investigate the progression of patients with myocardial infarction and their subsequent health outcomes. By applying a Markov model, we analyzed longitudinal data from patients who experienced a myocardial infarction and were followed for up to 10 years. Our results indicate that age and sex significantly influence the progression of patients with myocardial infarction, with men experiencing more rapid progression than women. This study demonstrates the potential of Multiple State Analysis to provide a more nuanced understanding of disease progression and to inform public health policy and clinical decision-making.

A novel multi-center quadrature scheme is developed for efficiently and accurately evaluating integrals over the continuum. The scheme employs a combination of discrete and continuous components, allowing for a more precise representation of integrals involving the Coulomb potential. By applying a specific quadrature rule to these integrals, the method achieves high precision and efficiency, even for complex systems. The performance of the new scheme is demonstrated through a series of benchmark tests, including comparisons with existing methods. The results show that the approach can significantly reduce computational costs while maintaining high precision, making it a valuable tool for high-precision calculations in quantum chemistry.

The vertices of a graph G can be partitioned into a subset S, where the distance between any two distinct vertices that are not in S can be uniquely determined by the distance to their nearest neighbors in S. The minimum size of S that satisfies this condition is known as the metric dimension of G, denoted by $\dim(G)$. This problem involves finding the minimum size of S, which is a known NP-hard problem. A parameterized algorithm for this problem was previously developed by Chen et al. with a time complexity of $O(2^{O((\text{treewidth}(G))^2)} \cdot n^3)$. This algorithm's running time depends heavily on treewidth, a parameter that measures the complexity of graph decomposition. In this paper, a new algorithm is developed that combines treewidth and feedback vertex set, a parameter that measures the complexity of graph decomposition by removing a subset of vertices that are part of all cycles. The new algorithm has a time complexity of $O(2^{O((\text{feedback vertex set})^2 \cdot \log(\text{feedback vertex set}) + \text{treewidth}(G)^3)} \cdot n)$. This algorithm's running time depends on the size of the graph, denoted by n, and the size of the subset S, which is a function of the other parameters. A directed space, or lub-space, is a topological space with filters whose limits are unique.  We investigate the power structures of lub-spaces, specifically the frame of closed subsets forming a complete lattice and the frame of all subsets forming an extensive ordered power structure.  We also examine the frames of closed and all subsets for directed complete partial orders, establishing them as complete lattices.  Additionally, we establish a comprehensive framework for equipping frames with a lub-structure, thereby enabling the construction of an extensive power structure on any frame.

Previous studies on Earth's climate have shown that atmospheric moisture can lead to
climate-driven water delivery to the surface, which can cause water-weather events.
These events can have a significant impact on the evolution of life and the development
of ecosystems. In this study, we have conducted simulations of Earth's hothouse climate
during its past warm periods, which were characterized by high temperatures and
reduced ice cover. Our results indicate that water delivery to the surface can still
occur even at high temperatures, leading to large water delivery events that can
potentially cause significant damage to the environment. Our findings suggest that
water-weather events can be an important factor in shaping the evolution of life and
the development of ecosystems, even in environments that are characterized by high
temperatures.

We've developed a spinor twistor approach to self-dual Yang-Mills theory, which can be further extended to incorporate higher-spin fields through the utilization of twistor holomorphic vector bundles. This method enables us to express the corresponding self-dual equations in the ambient space of twistor lines via pull-backs of holomorphic data. Additionally, we explore the spinor twistor approach in detail for self-dual solutions in the context of the anti-de Sitter space of conformal dimension four.

Deep learning models' performance in medical image classification is severely impacted by label noise, which is often exacerbated by the absence of a mechanism to correct noisy labels during training. In this study, we propose an innovative method that rectifies label noise in medical image classification by employing Bayesian statistics to assess the reliability of existing labels. A likelihood function is used to determine label reliability, which is then leveraged in conjunction with image features to adjust the classification model's parameters and improve its accuracy. Our approach, dubbed BRL, is tested on three datasets with artificially introduced label noise, demonstrating its ability to outperform state-of-the-art methods in mitigating the effects of noisy labels.

Consider a unit cube $Q^n$ in the $n$-dimensional space, and a function $f$ defined over this cube, belonging to the space $L^p(Q^n)$. The function can be approximated by $I^n f$, its tensor product interpolation, using values of $f$ at the vertices of $Q^n$. The aim of this study is to establish an estimate for the ratio between the estimated value and the actual function, specifically, to bound the expression $\frac{I^n f}{f}$ in the space $L^p(Q^n)$.

A correlated random walk (CRW) is a Markov chain that occurs on a graph, where the walker's movement is influenced by the direction it came from. This type of walk has been found to be useful in modeling real-world phenomena, such as the movement of animals, where the path an animal takes is often dependent on the path it took previously. In this study, we derive a characteristic polynomial for the transition probability matrix of a specific type of CRW, where the walk occurs on a graph that has a specific type of symmetry. Our results reveal that the eigenvalues of the transition probability matrix are determined by the roots of the derived polynomial, which can be used to analyze the long-term behavior of the CRW. Our analysis relies on the development of a specific type of matrix, which has a rich algebraic and geometric interpretation.

In a total functions logic like HOL, certain non-terminating functions are inaccessible to definition. However, for total functions, there are often equivalent terminating versions. This paper introduces a method to find such a terminating alternative, specifically for a single function. This approach allows for the creation of a new definition that's functionally identical to the original, but with a limited scope of variables. This new definition can then be used to simplify the original, leading to the creation of an optimized version of the function. This process can be repeated until no non-terminating calls remain.

To improve the accuracy of the models that predict the instantaneous state of wall-bounded flows, a new approach is developed by linking the model's parameters to specific characteristics of the flow.  By analyzing the relationship between the model's parameters and the energy distribution of the flow's dominant modes, a data-driven enhancement is achieved.  This enhancement is further refined by normalizing the model's parameters and correlating them with the location of the maximum energy in the Fourier spectrum.  As a result, the model's predictive capabilities are significantly improved, with the prediction errors for key flow statistics such as velocity and acceleration being reduced by up to 50%.  The improved model is also able to provide a more accurate representation of the flow's dynamics, including the evolution of the flow's dominant modes.

This research investigates self-dual (topological) solitons within a modified baby Skyrme model, derived from the Born-Infeld electromagnetic theory, and reveals that these solitons adhere to a self-dual equation, enabling the total energy to achieve a theoretical lower bound. Additionally, the study explores the characteristics of the resulting self-dual solitons through specific examples.

Investigating a Weyl semimetal model on a square lattice under the influence of strong magnetic fields, our findings indicate that the Hamiltonian can be simplified into four separate parts, each representing a Weyl equation. This leads to the creation of Weyl nodes in momentum space, where they appear as pairs with opposite chirality. However, the introduction of magnetic flux causes the Weyl nodes to split into Weyl arcs, which then transition into loops when the field strength is increased further. Additionally, our research shows that the Luttinger surfaces in this system exhibit a unique oscillation pattern in response to changes in magnetic flux.

We have developed a novel nanoantenna design that combines multiple materials to create highly efficient photon sources. This innovative hybrid nanoantenna, consisting of a gold disk and a silicon ring, is highly responsive to light across a wide range of wavelengths. By incorporating this nanoantenna into quantum dot emitters, we can significantly boost their brightness and increase the rate of photon emission by over 100 times. Our simulations demonstrate that this setup can produce single photons at a rate of nearly 250 million per second and achieve high levels of non-classical behavior.

The phenomenon of anomalous screening in granular matter is a well-documented effect, observed when a small amount of force is applied to a collection of particles, causing the larger particles to move in a specific direction. This effect has been studied extensively, but its theoretical understanding is still incomplete. In this work, we present experimental evidence and numerical simulations that support the idea that the anomalous screening effect can be explained by the interplay between the large and small particles, with the larger particles acting as a screen for the smaller particles, thus reducing the overall effect. The results of our study suggest that the anomalous screening effect can be used to control the flow of granular matter, with potential applications in the design of new types of granular devices.

Our research focuses on the electronic properties of silicene modified with manganese atoms, supported by a boron nitride substrate. Utilizing density functional theory, we investigated the stability of this structure and found that the manganese atoms prefer to bond with silicon atoms, resulting in a significant increase in the buckling of the silicene layer. The resulting structure exhibits a unique electronic configuration, characterized as a semiconductor with a direct band gap located at the K point in the Brillouin zone. The direct band gap can be easily adjusted by applying external pressure or tensile strain, offering potential for the development of novel electronic devices.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, has long been a subject of debate regarding its origin. Researchers have proposed two main theories: a supernova that occurred shortly before 1975, or a massive star that experienced a much older eruption in 1600 AD. To investigate these hypotheses, researchers analyzed infrared and X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Spitzer Space Telescope. The results suggest that the shock waves from the supernova are still expanding at a significant speed, around 1000 kilometers per second. This finding supports the idea that the supernova occurred in the early 20th century, rather than the much older 1600 AD event. Additionally, the data reveal that the supernova's explosion site is located near the center of the remnant, close to the Sgr A West supernova that occurred in 1975.

In the realm of machine learning, handling imbalanced data is a significant challenge, particularly in text classification tasks where class imbalance is a common issue. This problem can lead to suboptimal model performance, as models tend to favor majority classes. To address this, data augmentation techniques have been developed to create new samples for underrepresented classes. This study compares the effectiveness of various synthetic oversampling methods, such as SMOTE, for improving multi-class text classification. By evaluating these methods using different metrics, such as accuracy and F1-score, we aim to identify the most suitable augmentation technique for text classification tasks.

This study investigates the correlation between local news coverage and COVID-19 cases, deaths, and their respective audiences. Data from 159 U.S. counties was collected between March 13 and August 1, 2020, to examine the interplay between news and health outcomes. Key findings indicate that increased local news coverage was associated with higher COVID-19 cases, yet a decrease in deaths. Conversely, audiences who consumed more local news were likely to experience decreased cases and deaths. Notably, the study highlights the importance of local news in disseminating vital information during the pandemic.

A novel approach to preserving angular momentum in the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) algorithm has been developed. Conventional FMM algorithms do not guarantee conservation of angular momentum due to inaccuracies in approximating long-range particle interactions. Our new method ensures conservation of angular momentum within the algorithm by utilizing torque cancellation during the translation of multipole and local coefficients, thereby achieving exact angular momentum conservation in FMM.

A well-known issue in the field of reinforcement learning is the limited capacity of agents to learn from relatively small datasets. This limitation is particularly significant in applications where data collection is costly or time-consuming. One potential solution to this problem is the utilization of neural networks that can effectively generalize from learned patterns. This study investigates the use of a specific type of network, known as the multi-expert network, to improve the ability of agents to learn from small datasets. By employing an efficient data augmentation technique, the research demonstrates that multi-expert networks can learn policies that are comparable to those learned from substantially larger datasets. This capability is demonstrated through experiments in both grid-world and Atari environments.

A study has been conducted to investigate the creation of a heavy Higgs boson paired with a W or Z boson using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The investigation focused on HH production in the context of vector boson fusion and single associated production, with Higgs bosons decaying into additional pairs of bosons. The data, collected from 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, was analyzed in conjunction with simulations to establish a baseline. The results showed no significant deviation from the expected standard model, with the most restrictive limits on HH production being set. The production cross-section was constrained to a maximum of 0.11 and 0.16 times the expected rate for various mass combinations of Higgs bosons. The study further explored the possibility of new physics in the form of an effective dimension-6 operator in the SM effective field theory, with the most restrictive limits being set on the coupling between the W or Z boson and Higgs bosons.

Atomic vapor spin masers have been a subject of research for over 70 years, with recent advancements in technology driving renewed interest. Our work focuses on the development of a digital maser device that utilizes digital signal processing to extend the functionality of traditional analog masers. We have successfully implemented a digital maser based on Rb D1 transition, achieving a 2π/3 phase shift per loop iteration. This digital transformation offers significant advantages, including enhanced flexibility and the ability to integrate with other digital systems.
